newsitem.title: USA: Automakers say tough to meet Calif. electric car goal.
newsitem.headline: Automakers say tough to meet Calif. electric car goal.

text.p: Automakers have barely begun to sell electric cars in California, but they are already pessimistic about meeting the state's mandate that 10 percent of vehicles sold there be electric-powered by 2003.

At a news briefing Monday, executives for several automakers said they would not be able to meet the goal unless battery makers make big breakthroughs to lower cost and extend a car's range on a charge.
"Ten percent is a good long-range goal, but 2003, that's a pretty short time frame," said Frank Schweibold, platform finance director for GM's advanced technology.

Based on its 1996 sales of 355,453 units, GM would have to sell more than 35,000 electric vehicles to meet the California mandate. It has delivered 185 EV1 electric cars since it began marketing the teardrop-shaped two-seater to December.
Industry sales of electric vehicles in California would have to be 100,000 to 150,000 in 2003 to meet the state mandate.

The California Air Resources Board already has given automakers one reprieve, dropping mandates that 2 percent of vehicles sold in the state be electric by 1998 and 5 percent be electric by 2001. But the 2003 mandate of 10 percent was not changed, creating a big challenge for automakers.

Honda Motor Co. Ltd., the only other automaker to target consumers, is just beginning to sell its EV Plus electric cars. Robert Bienenfeld, manager of alternative fuel vehicle marketing for American Honda Motor Co. Inc., said the company expects to deliver about 10 to 15 of the cars a month.
"We're just in the process of learning who the cusomers are," he said. Volume will be determined in part by the performance of the technology, infrastructure and affordability, he added.

Honda is using nickel-metal hydride batteries, which provide longer-range than the traditional lead-acid batteries used in GM's EV1, and Ford Motor Co.'s electric Ranger pickup truck and Chrysler Corp.'s electric minivan, which are being marketed to large buyers such as car rental companies.

All automakers except Nissan Motor Co. Ltd. are planning to make an eventual switch to the nickel-metal hydride batteries. Nissan plans to introduce a compact van powered by lithium-ion batteries for the U.S. market in December.
Toyota Motor Corp. will begin deliveries of a two-door RAV4 sport utility vehicle with nickel-metal hydride batteries to large customers late this year.

But the new-generation batteries are still far too expensive to allow automakers to sell electric vehicles in big volumes. Ford's electric Ranger is priced at $32,975 with the cheaper lead-acid batteries.

"Our ability to sell in volume is totally dependent on our suppliers' ability to get in us a battery that will perform and be affordable in numbers," said John Wallace, Ford's director of Alternative Fuel Vehicles.
But executives also said they hoped that California would change the mandate to include other so-called "clean" vehicles in the mandate, including natural gas-powered vehicles and hybrid vehicles.
Towards the end of the decade, the state board and industry officials are to review the progress of electric vehicle development, after which changes could be made.
